explanations.answer: Aaron with Nadab and Abihu plus seventy elders
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD names Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), and Nadab and Abihu are Aaron's sons (Exodus 6:23). That's quite a crowd for one mountain trip. I can't even get three cookies to leave the cooling rack on time.

explanations.answer: Miriam with Jethro and Zipporah plus twelve leaders
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not the LORD's list. In Exodus 24:1 He names Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders. Seventy, not twelve. When a list has that many names, I read it twice and still hand over the wrong tray.

explanations.answer: Bezalel with Oholiab and Korah plus twelve spies
explanations.explanation: Nope, none of those names are on the LORD's list. He says Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Don't worry, baker, I've mixed up a guest list or two myself.

Right on the money, baker. The LORD says, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). They're invited up the mountain, and they worship from a distance. I think that's a lot to take in, being invited and told to keep your spot all at once.

Almost, baker, but this one is True. The LORD tells the group, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). So they come up the mountain, and they worship at a distance. I once guessed the wrong way on a card like this, and my mustache drooped for an hour.

I see why you'd think so, baker, but this one is False. The LORD says, “And the people may not go up with him.” (Exodus 24:2). Moses alone approaches the LORD, and the others must not come near. The people stay down below.

That's it, friend. The LORD says, “And the people may not go up with him.” (Exodus 24:2). Moses alone approaches the LORD, and the others must not come near. The people stay down below, and the line for this mountain is very short.

That's the word, baker. The people all respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). One voice, all of them together. Even my kitchen has never agreed on anything that fast.

Good try, but no weighing in this verse. The people respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). The word is do. I do my weighing with flour, baker, and even that takes me two tries.

No discussion in this verse, friend. The people all respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). The word is do. One voice, all together, and nobody asking for a meeting.

Not quite, baker. Moses builds the altar at the base of the mountain, not at the top (Exodus 24:4). He gets up early the next morning and builds it at the bottom. That's a lot of stairs I'm glad he didn't take for this one.

You got it, baker. Moses gets up early the next morning and builds the altar at the base of the mountain (Exodus 24:4). It's at the bottom, near the people, not way up at the top. My own shortcuts have never been that smart.

That's a keeper, baker. Moses builds the altar along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 24:4). One pillar for each tribe, standing at the base of the mountain. I'd need a chart just to keep my cookie cutters in order, and I only have six.

Good guess, but the text gives a different answer. Moses builds twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 24:4). The pillars stand for the tribes, not the plagues. I always count twice when I'm stamping a dozen.

The text says something else, friend. Moses builds twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 24:4). So each pillar stands for one of the tribes. Seven is a good number, but this verse is counting twelve.

Yes, baker. Moses sends out some young men of Israel, and they offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). The text just says young men of Israel. It doesn't say more about who they are, so I won't guess.

Not this time, baker. The text says Moses sends out some young men of Israel (Exodus 24:5). It doesn't name Aaron or his sons for this job. I'll stick with what the verse says and keep my guesses in the oven.

Good thinking, but the text says something else. Moses sends out some young men of Israel to offer the offerings (Exodus 24:5). It doesn't say tribal leaders. Young men of Israel, that's the whole description.

That's right, baker. The young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). The text puts the bulls and the peace offerings together right there. A big day for the altar, I'd say.

This one is True, baker. The text says the young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). So the bulls are right there in the verse. I've second-guessed a True before and felt like a flat cookie.

Perfect aim, baker. Moses takes half of the blood and puts it in bowls, and the other half he splatters on the altar (Exodus 24:6). Two halves, two places. If I tried that with sprinkles, the whole counter would know.

Close, baker, since the pillars are right there too. But the text says Moses splatters the other half of the blood on the altar (Exodus 24:6). The pillars stand for the twelve tribes, and the altar gets the blood. I mix up my toppings sometimes too.
Not the ground, friend. Moses puts half of the blood in bowls and splatters the other half on the altar (Exodus 24:6). The altar is where it goes. I'd have swept the floor twice if it were me.

explanations.answer: He splatters it on the people
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). That comes right after the people promise to do what the LORD has spoken (Exodus 24:7). It's a serious moment, so I'll just stand here quietly with my mustache.

explanations.answer: He carries it up the mountain
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but that's not what the text says. Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). The blood goes on the people, not up the mountain. Moses doesn't leave them out of this.

explanations.answer: He sets it before the elders
explanations.explanation: Not the elders, friend. The text says Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). It's the people who get it, and Moses says what it means. I'd have needed a bigger bowl and a longer memory.

That's a keeper, baker. Moses goes up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-10). The text says they saw Him, plain as that. I'll keep my jokes down for this one.

Good thinking, but the text says something different. In Exodus 24:10, Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel. There's no bush in this verse. I don't have a joke for this one, baker, only the verse.

That's a fun image, baker, but it's not in this verse. The text says Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:10). Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire. I'd stick to the verse, since my oven is the only fire I trust.

Not this time, baker. The text says, “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). They saw Him and they're still sitting there. It's a good thing I checked my notes before I got worried.

That's it, baker. “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). They saw Him and stayed right where they were. I'm relieved, and my mustache is too.
Box-worthy, baker. The text says, “…they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). Eating and drinking, right there. I'd have been taking notes on the menu, but the text doesn't give one.
Fun guess, baker, but it's not in the text. Exodus 24:11 says, “…they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” So they eat and drink. Singing and dancing isn't mentioned there.
That's not what the text says, friend. Exodus 24:11 says, “…they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” They eat and drink. I'd have dropped my spatula, but the text doesn't say anyone dropped anything.

That's it, baker. The LORD says He will give Moses the tablets of stone, “with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). Instruction is the word the LORD uses. I've been learning my own lessons from this book ever since I left that drawer.

Not judgment, friend. The LORD says the tablets hold “the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). The word is instruction. I'll stick with what the LORD said and leave my own guessing for the dough.

Good word, but it's not the one the LORD uses. He says, “…the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). The word is instruction. Protection is a fine word too, but I only quote what's on the page.

That's a keeper, baker. Moses sets out with Joshua his attendant and goes up on the mountain of God (Exodus 24:13). Joshua already fought the Amalekites for Israel (Exodus 17:10). Joshua is the only one the text names for this part of the climb.

Not this one, baker. The text says Moses went up with Joshua his attendant (Exodus 24:13). It doesn't name anyone else on this part of the climb. I'd bring snacks for the trip, but the text doesn't mention any.
Close, but the text names someone else. Moses sets out with Joshua his attendant (Exodus 24:13). Joshua fought the Amalekites for Israel (Exodus 17:10). Nobody else is named here, baker.

You got it, baker. Moses tells the elders, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (Exodus 24:14). Hur is the man who helped hold up Moses' hands in a battle (Exodus 17:12). I think Moses picked folks he could count on, and that makes me smile.

Not those two, baker. The text says Moses tells the elders, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (Exodus 24:14). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Hur is the man who helped hold up Moses' hands in a battle (Exodus 17:12).

That's a fun pair of names, friend, but they're not in this verse. Moses tells the elders, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (Exodus 24:14). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Hur is the man who helped hold up Moses' hands in a battle (Exodus 17:12).

Perfect, baker. The cloud covers the mountain for six days, and “on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.” (Exodus 24:16). Six days, then the LORD calls. I'd have checked the oven six times, but this is a different kind of waiting.

This one is True, baker. Exodus 24:16 says the cloud covered the mountain for six days, “and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.” So the LORD calls on the seventh day. Waiting is hard, and I've had my own long waits.

Baked just right, baker. The text says, “And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). Like a consuming fire, that's the text's own comparison. I know a lot about fire, and I'll let this verse speak for itself.

Not a storm, baker. The text says the sight of the glory of the LORD “was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). The comparison is fire. I'll leave the weather forecast to somebody else.

Not a flood, friend. The text says the sight of the glory of the LORD “was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). It says fire, and it says it's what the Israelites saw. I'd stay with the verse, baker.
That's a keeper, baker. Moses “remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). That's a long stretch on one mountain. My longest wait was in a drawer, and I'd still take his.

Close, since seven shows up in the passage, but not for this. The cloud covered the mountain for six days, and on the seventh the LORD called to Moses (Exodus 24:16). After that, Moses “remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). Forty is the number here.
Not three, baker. The text says Moses “remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). That's a lot longer than three. I'd have run out of cookies and patience.
